ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rotation-based steering in the normalised activation plane
PROPOSAL: We define steering as a rotation of each residual activation within the plane spanned by its own direction and a refusal direction estimated from contrastive prompts, with the rotation angle as the only control parameter. Because the next block applies RMS normalisation, a rotation changes direction while leaving norm unchanged, so one angle works at every layer. We sweep the angle from zero to a full half-turn on open instruction-tuned models of three sizes and record refusal rates on harmful prompts and compliance on harmless ones.
CONTROLS: Activation addition with per-layer tuned coefficients, directional ablation, and the unsteered model, with perplexity on held-out text and accuracy on a general knowledge benchmark at each angle.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Refusal should vary smoothly and monotonically with the angle while perplexity stays flat. Models whose refusal is not captured by a single direction may show jumps instead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A common geometric framework for addition, ablation and rotation steering
PROPOSAL: We write activation addition, directional ablation and rotation as maps on the unit sphere obtained after RMS normalisation and derive, for each, the induced change in cosine with the feature direction and with unrelated directions. We then verify the predictions empirically on two open model families by measuring how each operation shifts the projections onto a bank of probe directions for sentiment, topic and language that the edit is not meant to touch.
CONTROLS: Random directions of equal norm as edits, the unedited model, and the same measurements taken before and after normalisation to confirm the role of the rescaling.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: Rotation should leave projections on unrelated directions nearly unchanged, while addition at large coefficients should disturb them. Where feature directions are far from orthogonal, every operation will leak into neighbouring features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Restricting steering edits to a two-dimensional subspace
PROPOSAL: We restrict every steering edit to the plane formed by the target feature direction and the component of the activation orthogonal to it, leaving the remaining dimensions exactly as they were. This should protect unrelated features stored elsewhere in the representation. We implement the restriction for refusal and for emotion steering on models from two families and three sizes, measuring how general benchmarks change across the full range of steering strength.
CONTROLS: Unrestricted activation addition at matched effect on the target behaviour, ablation along the same direction, and a restriction to a random plane as placebo, with language modelling loss, multiple-choice accuracy and a fluency judge.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: Plane-restricted edits should keep general benchmarks within noise of the unsteered model over the whole range. Behaviours encoded across several directions would escape a single plane and limit control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tracing the transition from refusal to compliance under graded steering
PROPOSAL: We steer instruction-tuned models along a refusal direction in many small increments and, at every step, record the full response to a fixed set of harmful requests, classifying it into refusal, partial refusal with caveats, hedged compliance, and full compliance. This reveals whether intermediate behaviours exist or whether the model switches abruptly. We repeat the analysis across layers to locate where the transition is sharpest.
CONTROLS: The same increments along random directions, the unsteered model sampled at several temperatures to separate steering from sampling noise, and a second annotator to check the response categories.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: We expect a graded sequence of intermediate behaviours rather than a single switch. Some prompts may still flip at a narrow range of strengths, pointing to thresholds in later layers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Steering emotion and refusal with one angle-based control across model families
PROPOSAL: We estimate directions for refusal and for six emotions from contrastive prompt sets and apply angle-based steering at all layers of models from four families ranging from one to seventy billion parameters. We test whether a single angle setting transfers across families and sizes, and whether emotion steering obeys the same smooth control curve as refusal.
CONTROLS: Per-layer tuned activation addition, directional ablation, and the unsteered models, with an emotion classifier, a refusal judge, perplexity and a reading comprehension benchmark at each angle.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: The control curve should have the same shape across families for refusal, with emotions noisier but still monotonic. Small models may lack clean emotion directions, which would break transfer at the low end.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Norm growth across layers and the brittleness of addition coefficients
PROPOSAL: We measure activation norms layer by layer on several open models and show how a fixed addition coefficient translates into very different relative edits at shallow and deep layers. We then compare the steering effect of addition calibrated to each layer's norm with rotation by a fixed angle, which is insensitive to norm by construction, across refusal and sentiment behaviours.
CONTROLS: Uncalibrated addition with one global coefficient, norm-calibrated addition, rotation, and the unsteered model, each with perplexity and target behaviour rates on held-out prompts.
COST: 110
PREDICTION: Norm-calibrated addition should close much of the gap to rotation, but rotation should remain the easiest to set. Layers right after large norm jumps may still behave erratically for every method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional angular steering that acts only on relevant inputs
PROPOSAL: We combine a lightweight detector, which reads the projection of the activation on the refusal direction, with rotation steering applied only when the projection exceeds a threshold. This keeps benign prompts untouched while allowing graded control on borderline and harmful prompts. We compare false refusal rates and harmful compliance rates on mixed benchmarks of benign and harmful requests across two model sizes.
CONTROLS: Unconditional rotation at the same angle, conditional activation addition with the same detector, and the unsteered model, with general capability benchmarks run on benign prompts only.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Conditional rotation should lower false refusals compared to unconditional rotation at similar control over harmful prompts. Detector errors near the threshold could produce inconsistent behaviour on borderline prompts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inverting a behaviour by rotating past the orthogonal complement
PROPOSAL: Test whether rotating activations beyond the orthogonal complement of a feature direction induces the opposite behaviour, for example eager compliance turning into refusal of benign requests, or joy turning into sadness. We apply rotations at angles past a quarter-turn on two model families and measure behaviour on paired benign and harmful prompt sets and on emotion prompts.
CONTROLS: Ablation, which stops at the complement, negative activation addition at matched projection change, and rotations of the same angle in a random plane.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Rotations past the complement should produce the opposite behaviour in a dose-dependent way for refusal and emotions alike. Fluency may drop at the largest angles, limiting how far inversion can go.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Do steering directions estimated on one dataset control behaviour on another
PROPOSAL: We estimate refusal and emotion directions from one contrastive prompt collection and evaluate graded steering with them on several other collections that differ in topic, length and phrasing. The study checks whether the continuous control curve obtained on the estimation set holds out of distribution, which matters if such interventions are to be applied broadly.
CONTROLS: Directions re-estimated on each target collection as an upper reference, random directions as a lower reference, and the unsteered model, with behaviour classifiers and perplexity.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Out-of-distribution control should follow the same curve with a modest shift in the angle needed for a given effect. Topics far from the estimation set may need their own directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring collateral damage of steering on unrelated capabilities
PROPOSAL: We build an evaluation suite that measures what steering does to everything other than its target: factual recall, arithmetic, code completion, multilingual translation and long-context retrieval. Each steering method is applied at the strength needed to reach a fixed change in the target behaviour, and the suite reports the change in each capability relative to the unsteered model.
CONTROLS: The unsteered model with resampling to estimate noise, random-direction edits with matched norm, and the target behaviour measured on the same prompts for every method.
COST: 230
PREDICTION: Rotation within a plane should show the smallest losses at matched effect, addition the largest. Long-context retrieval may be the most fragile capability for all methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Angle-controlled steering checked against tuned addition and ablation
PROPOSAL: We rotate residual activations toward or away from a refusal direction within the plane they span, using a single angle that should work at every layer after RMS normalisation. We ask whether this gives smooth control from full refusal to compliance, so each angle is compared with the existing operations at equal effect on the target.
CONTROLS: Activation addition with per-layer tuned coefficients and directional ablation at matched refusal rate, rotations in random planes as placebo, the unsteered model, and perplexity plus a general benchmark at every angle, over three prompt splits.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: Rotation should give a monotonic refusal curve with flat perplexity, while addition degrades fluency at strong settings. Jumps in the curve would suggest refusal spreads over several directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Angle-controlled steering of refusal in instruction-tuned language models
PROPOSAL: We rotate residual activations toward or away from a refusal direction within the plane they span, with a single angle as the control parameter at every layer. We sweep the angle over a fine grid and record refusal rates on a public set of harmful prompts, reporting the resulting curve for two model sizes.
CONTROLS: Two grid resolutions for the angle sweep, the refusal judge prompted in two wordings, a check that outputs remain in English, the curve recomputed with a second decoding temperature, and a baseline run at angle zero.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: Refusal should change smoothly as the angle grows from zero to a half-turn. The curve may flatten near the ends where the model already refuses or complies fully.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Does plane-restricted steering spare unrelated features
PROPOSAL: We confine steering edits to the two-dimensional plane of the target direction and the activation, leaving all other components intact, and test whether unrelated features survive. To see that, we track a bank of probe directions for topic, sentiment and language that the edit should not affect, and general capabilities across the full steering range.
CONTROLS: Unrestricted addition at matched target effect, ablation along the same direction, a random plane of the same dimension, the unsteered model, and probe readings, perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy, each with resampling noise estimates.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: Plane-restricted edits should leave probe readings and benchmarks within noise of the unsteered model. If unrelated probes shift as much as with addition, the restriction brings no protection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Plane-restricted steering edits for refusal and emotion control
PROPOSAL: We confine steering edits to the two-dimensional plane of the target direction and the activation, leaving the other components intact, and apply this to refusal and emotion steering. We record target behaviour across the steering range on two model families and inspect sample outputs for coherence at the strongest settings.
CONTROLS: The restricted method at two estimation set sizes for the direction, layers chosen by two heuristics, an ablation of the prompt template used to estimate the direction, and a fluency rating of ten outputs per setting.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: Target behaviour should follow the steering strength closely on both families. Outputs may become repetitive at the strongest settings for the smaller model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer of one angle setting across model families and sizes
PROPOSAL: We test whether a single rotation angle yields the same behavioural effect on models from four families and several sizes, which is required for steering to be broadly applicable. For each model we estimate the refusal direction on the same contrastive prompts and apply identical angles at all layers.
CONTROLS: Per-model tuned addition coefficients as a reference for what tuning buys, directional ablation, random-plane rotations, the unsteered models, and a second behaviour, sentiment, to check that transfer is not specific to refusal.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: The same angle should give similar refusal rates across families, within a few points. Large departures in one family would show that the angle does not transfer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Applying one angle setting to models from several families
PROPOSAL: We apply a single rotation angle to models from four families and several sizes, estimating the refusal direction for each model on the same contrastive prompts and steering at all layers. We report refusal rates per model at the chosen angle together with example generations from each family.
CONTROLS: Two random seeds for the prompt sampling, the same angle applied at a subset of middle layers, a comparison of two chat templates, the refusal judge run twice to check consistency, and output length per model.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Refusal rates should be broadly similar across families at the chosen angle. The smallest models may be less responsive to steering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graded transition between refusal and compliance under fine steering steps
PROPOSAL: We steer models along a refusal direction in many small steps and classify each response to fixed harmful requests into full refusal, refusal with caveats, hedged compliance or full compliance, to see whether behaviour changes gradually or switches. Sampling noise could mimic gradual change, so we separate the two explicitly.
CONTROLS: The unsteered model sampled many times per prompt to measure the spread due to sampling, steps along random directions, a second annotator with agreement statistics, and the same sweep on benign prompts to separate refusal from general degradation.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Intermediate categories should rise and fall in sequence as strength grows, beyond what sampling alone produces. A step-like curve would favour a switch-like mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fine-step sweep of refusal steering on harmful requests
PROPOSAL: We steer models along a refusal direction in many small steps and classify each response to fixed harmful requests into full refusal, refusal with caveats, hedged compliance or full compliance. We plot the share of each category across the sweep for two models and discuss the shape of the transition from refusal to compliance.
CONTROLS: Step sizes of two granularities, the sweep repeated at the first and last third of the layers, an ablation of the system prompt, two decoding lengths, and the categories also assigned by an automatic classifier.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Intermediate categories should appear between refusal and compliance as strength grows. Their share may differ between the two models because of different safety tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Collateral effects of steering measured at matched target effect
PROPOSAL: We compare rotation, addition and ablation on what they do to abilities outside the target behaviour, which is the core requirement of non-destructive control. Each method runs at the strength reaching the same refusal change, and we score factual recall, arithmetic, translation and long-context retrieval.
CONTROLS: Matching on target effect rather than on coefficient, the unsteered model with repeated sampling as noise floor, random-direction edits of equal norm, and a second target behaviour, emotion, to check that the ranking holds beyond refusal.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Rotation should lose the least capability at matched effect. If rankings change between refusal and emotion, the protection depends on the behaviour.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effects of rotation steering on general abilities of language models
PROPOSAL: We apply rotation steering for refusal at a fixed angle and score the steered model on factual recall, arithmetic, translation and long-context retrieval, to document what this form of control does to general abilities. Results appear as a capability table for two open model sizes.
CONTROLS: Two prompt formats for each capability benchmark, results with and without few-shot examples, a comparison of greedy and sampled decoding, and per-task output length to check that answers are complete.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Most capabilities should stay close to the scores published for the base models. Long-context retrieval may drop the most under steering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rotation in the normalised plane as a scale-free steering control
PROPOSAL: We exploit the fact that RMS normalisation keeps only the direction of an activation, and define steering as a rotation toward or away from the feature direction by an angle, which unifies ablation at a quarter-turn and inversion beyond it. One parameter should then govern expression from full to inverted at any layer. We test smoothness and layer independence on refusal and emotion.
CONTROLS: Per-layer tuned addition, ablation, random-plane rotations, and the unsteered model, with perplexity and a general benchmark at every angle.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Behaviour should vary smoothly with angle, and the same angle should work across layers. Behaviours spread over several directions would blur the fit.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Steering by fine-tuning low-rank adapters on contrastive pairs
PROPOSAL: We train low-rank adapters on contrastive pairs of refusing and complying responses, and interpolate between the base and adapted weights with a mixing coefficient that serves as the control parameter. One parameter should then govern expression from full to absent at any layer. We test smoothness and layer independence on refusal and emotion.
CONTROLS: Per-layer tuned addition, ablation, adapters trained on shuffled pairs, and the unsteered model, with perplexity and a general benchmark at every coefficient.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Behaviour should vary smoothly with the mixing coefficient on both tasks. Interpolated weights may lose fluency in the middle of the range.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Isolating the target feature from unrelated features during steering
PROPOSAL: We restrict every edit to the plane of the target direction and the current activation, so that components along unrelated feature directions remain exactly unchanged, and we measure whether general abilities survive across the whole control range. This directly targets interference between features sharing the same representation.
CONTROLS: Unrestricted addition at matched target effect, ablation, a random-plane restriction, and probe readings for unrelated features with perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy at every strength.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Unrelated probe readings and benchmarks should stay within noise across the whole range. Strongly entangled features would still move.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reducing interference by steering only at the final layer
PROPOSAL: We apply steering edits only at the final layer before the output head, on the view that later computation then has no chance to spread the edit to other features, and we measure whether general abilities survive across the whole control range. This aims at interference between features sharing the same representation.
CONTROLS: Steering at all layers at matched target effect, ablation, steering at a random layer, and probe readings for unrelated features with perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy at every strength.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: General abilities should hold since few layers are touched. The target behaviour may be hard to reach from the final layer alone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Behaviour along a continuous path from refusal to compliance
PROPOSAL: We rotate activations in small angular steps between the refusal direction and its opposite and analyse responses to harmful requests at each step, measuring how often intermediate behaviours such as partial refusal with safety caveats appear. This characterises the continuous change the question asks about rather than an on and off switch.
CONTROLS: Repeated sampling of the unsteered model to measure noise, random-plane rotations, a second annotator, and benign prompts to separate refusal changes from general degradation.
COST: 130
PREDICTION: Intermediate behaviours should appear in a reproducible order along the path. A sudden switch would show that the behaviour is effectively binary.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparing refusal behaviour across safety-tuned and base models
PROPOSAL: We compare responses to harmful requests between instruction-tuned models and their base counterparts, measuring how often intermediate behaviours such as partial refusal with safety caveats appear in each, to understand how alignment training shapes the transition between refusing and complying.
CONTROLS: Repeated sampling of each model to measure noise, a second annotator, two prompt templates, and benign prompts to separate refusal changes from general degradation in tuning.
COST: 130
PREDICTION: Tuned models should show more intermediate behaviours than base models. Base models may comply with most requests regardless of phrasing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A unified account of addition, ablation and rotation under normalisation
PROPOSAL: We express the three steering primitives as maps on the unit sphere after RMS normalisation and derive what each does to the cosine with the target and with unrelated directions, making their limits explicit. We then confirm the derived effects on two model families by measuring projections on a bank of probe directions.
CONTROLS: Random edits of equal norm, the unedited model, and measurements before and after normalisation to confirm its role.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The framework should predict when addition overshoots and why ablation cannot invert. Mismatch between derived and measured effects would point to normalisation not being the dominant factor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A taxonomy of steering methods from published implementations
PROPOSAL: We survey published steering implementations and group them by where they intervene, how they estimate directions and which behaviours they target, producing a reference table that clarifies their respective scope. We then rerun three representative methods on two model families to check that reported behaviour changes reproduce.
CONTROLS: Random edits of equal norm, the unedited model, and two seeds for each rerun to confirm stability.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The taxonomy should show that most methods intervene at middle layers with contrastive directions. Some reported effects may not reproduce on other families.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Steering emotions with the same angle control as refusal
PROPOSAL: We extend angle-based steering beyond refusal to six emotions and to formality, estimating each direction from contrastive prompts, and test whether control stays smooth, non-destructive and consistent across three model families and sizes. This addresses whether the approach is broadly applicable rather than tied to one behaviour.
CONTROLS: Per-layer tuned addition, ablation, random-plane rotations, the unsteered models, emotion and formality classifiers, and perplexity at every angle.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: Control curves for emotions should resemble the refusal curve in shape across families. Emotions with weak directions may show noisy control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Steering refusal through prompt prefixes learned by search
PROPOSAL: We search over short prompt prefixes that push refusal up or down, using a genetic search scored by a refusal judge, and test whether chaining prefixes of graded strength gives smooth, non-destructive control consistent across three model families and sizes. This aims to make control broadly applicable without access to internal states.
CONTROLS: Per-layer tuned addition, ablation, random prefixes of the same length, the unsteered models, a refusal classifier, and perplexity at every strength.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: Graded prefixes should move refusal in steps across families. Prefix effects may not transfer to emotions or other behaviours.
